text: Everything up to now has been building toward one moment: posting. This is where a journal stops being a draft and starts actually changing balances.

Three things have to be true first. The journal has to pass validation — balanced, valid accounts, open period. It has to clear its approval workflow, if one applies, or need no approval at all. And its accounting date has to fall in a period that's actually Open, not just Future Enterable.

Before posting, a journal's debits and credits are just a draft — they haven't touched a single balance. Posting updates the balances cube for every account the journal's lines touch. Take our office supplies accrual: post it, and accrued liabilities goes up by twelve-fifty, office supplies expense goes up by twelve-fifty, and cash — which this accrual never touched — is completely untouched.

You can post one batch right after completing it, or select several approved batches and post them together in one action — useful at month-end when a controller wants to clear a dozen batches in one pass. Either way, posting runs as a submitted process you monitor to completion, not an instant flip.

Once a journal posts, its lines are read-only — permanently. That's deliberate: a posted journal has already changed real balances, and quietly editing it afterward would make those balances untrustworthy. If a posted journal is wrong, the fix is a reversal, not an edit. That's lesson eleven: reversing journals.
